questions.text: Tell me about a product decision you made with incomplete data. How did you decide, and what happened?
questions.rationale: PM work is judgment under uncertainty; the story reveals the candidate's actual decision process.

questions.text: Walk me through how you validated a feature idea before building it. What did you do when the evidence was mixed?
questions.rationale: Screens for hypothesis-driven discovery discipline versus instinct-built roadmaps.

questions.text: Describe a feature you killed. How did you make the call and communicate it?
questions.rationale: Killing work is harder than starting it; this tests conviction and stakeholder care.

questions.text: How do you decide what NOT to build this quarter? Give a real example of something you deliberately deferred.
questions.rationale: Prioritization shows up more honestly in what was cut than in what was chosen.

questions.text: Tell me about a time engineering told you something was impossible in the timeframe. What did you do?
questions.rationale: Screens for collaborative negotiation with engineering rather than pressure or capitulation.

questions.text: Describe how you ran your most recent user research. Who did you talk to, and what changed as a result?
questions.rationale: Distinguishes PMs who actually talk to users from those who cite research secondhand.

questions.text: What is a product you admire and one specific decision its team made that you would have made differently?
questions.rationale: Tests product taste with enough specificity to prevent rehearsed answers.

questions.text: Walk me through a launch that went poorly. What did you miss and what did you change in your next launch?
questions.rationale: Postmortem honesty and applied learning matter more than a clean track record.

questions.text: How do you write a good problem statement? Walk me through one you wrote recently.
questions.rationale: The artifact-based follow-up catches candidates who describe best practice but do not practice it.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to say no to an important customer. How did you do it?
questions.rationale: Tests spine with customers and whether no comes with a path forward.

questions.text: Describe a metric you chose to measure a product's success and how it misled you.
questions.rationale: Sophistication about metric failure modes separates senior PMs from dashboard readers.

questions.text: How do you keep engineers connected to the why behind the roadmap? Give an example.
questions.rationale: Screens for whether the candidate treats engineers as partners or as a delivery function.

questions.text: What draws you to product management over the adjacent roles you could do?
questions.rationale: Tests self-awareness about the actual shape of PM work, glue work included.

questions.text: Tell me about the hardest stakeholder you have managed. What made it hard and what worked?
questions.rationale: Stakeholder difficulty is universal; the coping strategy reveals maturity.

questions.text: Describe a time you shipped an MVP that felt embarrassingly small. What did you learn from it?
questions.rationale: Screens for genuine comfort with validated learning over polish pride.

questions.text: How do you handle a sprint where everything is priority one according to leadership?
questions.rationale: Tests whether the candidate forces real prioritization or passes the chaos downstream.

questions.text: Walk me through a pricing or packaging decision you were part of. What data informed it?
questions.rationale: Commercial judgment is rare in PMs; a real pricing story evidences it.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you changed your roadmap because of a competitor's move. Or chose not to. Why?
questions.rationale: Screens for strategic composure versus reactive feature matching.

questions.text: How do you document decisions so the team does not relitigate them in three months?
questions.rationale: Decision hygiene is a learnable craft; this checks the candidate has one.

questions.text: Describe a time you were wrong about what users wanted. How did you find out?
questions.rationale: Tests intellectual humility and closeness to real user feedback loops.

questions.text: What would your last engineering counterpart say about working with you? What would they say you should improve?
questions.rationale: The second half of the question does the screening; evasive answers are informative.

questions.text: Walk me through how you would decide between two features when each has a vocal executive sponsor.
questions.rationale: Tests political navigation anchored to user and business value rather than power.

questions.text: Tell me about a B2B deal that pressured you to build something off-roadmap. What did you do?
questions.rationale: The one-customer-feature trap is a defining PM test in B2B companies.

questions.text: How do you know when discovery is done and it is time to commit to building?
questions.rationale: Screens for a working threshold between learning and shipping; both failure modes are costly.

questions.text: What is the most useful piece of feedback you have received about your product work?
questions.rationale: Feedback receptivity, evidenced by specificity of recall.

questions.text: Describe your experience with A/B testing. Tell me about a test whose result surprised you.
questions.rationale: Surprise stories indicate real experimentation; unsurprising results suggest confirmation exercises.

questions.text: As a group PM or lead, how do you develop the PMs under you? Give a specific example of someone you grew.
questions.rationale: People development stories separate genuine leads from senior ICs with the title.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you aligned three or more teams behind one goal. What almost derailed it?
questions.rationale: Cross-team alignment is the core lead-level skill; the near-derailment probes realism.

questions.text: What product problem in our space would you be most excited to own, and what is your first hypothesis about it?
questions.rationale: Tests preparation, genuine interest, and hypothesis-first thinking in one question.

questions.text: How do you balance qualitative signals against quantitative ones when they disagree? Give an example.
questions.rationale: The disagreement case is where judgment lives; either-or answers are a flag.
